stories.summary: Shaving absent-mindedly before the shoot, Amit nicked his lip, and the cut would not stop bleeding. Soon there was a trail of blood running down to his bare torso. Ajay, putting on a 'scientific hat', said oxygen makes blood clot and told him to stand in front of a fan. Amit asked whether a hairdryer would do, and ended up aiming one at his lips. He then turned the moment into the episode's frame: a single superficial cut clots and stops, but a body with a thousand deep cuts and no clotting mechanism just keeps bleeding.
stories.insight: India's pension promises are that second body: a fiscal wound with no built-in mechanism to stop the bleeding, and it compounds across generations.
stories.quote: But imagine a body where you have a thousand deep cuts and the mechanism of clotting isn't there, and it bleeds and it bleeds and it bleeds, and what's going to happen, right?

stories.topic: What Kept JP Narayan Up at Night
stories.summary: In his third Seen and the Unseen episode with the politician Jayaprakash Narayan, JP told Amit that the one issue keeping him awake was India's pensions crisis, because states were moving to replace the NPS with the Old Pension Scheme. Amit had never heard of either and didn't see the big deal. Following up, he found that Ajay was one of the architects of the NPS. That led to a Seen and the Unseen episode with Ajay and Renuka Sane, and the government's new UPS led to this one.
stories.insight: Some of the most consequential policy fights hide behind boring acronyms. When a seasoned reformer is this alarmed, it is worth digging in.
stories.quote: And he said, No, Amit, we are destroying our future generation.

stories.topic: From Port Workers' Charity to Bismarck's Pension
stories.summary: Pensions began as voluntary kindness. Port workers whose bodies were broken from lugging boxes got a little money pooled by the current workers when they retired. Bismarck turned this into state policy in 1889: 50% of the last year's income, paid from age 70. But this was a world with no antibiotics, where bloodletting with leeches was still practised. Few people reached 70 and those who did didn't live long after, so the promise cost almost nothing. Over the following century longevity rose, birth rates fell and democratic politics kept loosening the terms. The cheap gesture became a 'bloody mess' everywhere.
stories.insight: A promise that is nearly free when it is made can become ruinous decades later. The real cost of a pension sits in demographics and time, not in the announcement.
stories.quote: Now the economic materiality of this was very small because people died quickly. So it was just a polite thing that you do to older people.

stories.summary: By the 1990s, simple extrapolations of pension payouts in the civil service, railways and military showed they could not be afforded. In 1998, under the Vajpayee government, Anand Bordia, a joint secretary in the Ministry of Social Justice (Maneka Gandhi was the minister), worked with Gautam Bhardwaj to launch Project Oasis. It was led by Surendra Dave, founding chairman of SEBI, and Ajay sat on its expert committee. Bhardwaj and Dave then computed the implicit pension debt: the present value of the promises made to civil servants came to 68% of GDP. People had been watching payouts double every six years, but nobody had seen the size of the stock.
stories.insight: The same problem looks manageable as a yearly flow and terrifying as a stock. One correct calculation was enough to wake up a cabinet.
stories.quote: That was an eye opener and it helped wake up everybody on the scale of this problem.

stories.summary: Ajay was then in the Ministry of Finance. He recalls Vajpayee repeatedly asking for alternatives ('Suppose you do it like this, show me the calculations') before settling on a deal. Government employees got a 10% wage hike, and 20% of the new wage went into a personal pension account. Take-home pay went from 100 to 90, while 20 went into the employee's own account, in exchange for giving up the old defined-benefit promise.
stories.insight: Good reform pairs technical design with political judgment about what will feel fair to the people who bear it.
stories.quote: This was pure political judgment of Vajpayee.

stories.summary: Ajay worked directly with Yashwant Sinha, S Narayan and UK Sinha. S Narayan persuaded Jaswant Singh, and the two of them then persuaded Advani and Vajpayee. Ajay was not in the decisive cabinet meeting, but UK Sinha was. The 'big four' supported the reform and many other ministers opposed it. Vajpayee, who in meetings either appeared to be asleep or actually was ('you could never tell'), took in the debate and then ruled: 'Yeh to karna hi hai' (this simply has to be done). He signed the file on 12 December 2002, and from 1 January 2004 all new government employees joined the NPS.
stories.insight: Reforms that pay off over a century need leaders willing to bite the bullet for benefits no current voter will see.
stories.quote: So I want to put up Yeh to karna hi hai as the slogan for every dreamer, every reformer, every do-gooder in the country that you have to bite the bullet and you have to do these things.

stories.topic: The Crash That Helped Pick a Dream Team
stories.summary: During the 2004 campaign, one Congress candidate in Delhi tried to stir up fears that the NDA was taking away defined-benefit pensions, but it got no traction. On 17 May 2004, after some CPM politicians talked about tearing the house down, the stock market crashed. Ajay makes a causal claim: the crisis helped Sonia Gandhi settle on Manmohan Singh, P Chidambaram, Montek Ahluwalia and C Rangarajan, which calmed markets. The new UPA government then re-examined the NDA's pension decision from scratch and kept it.
stories.insight: A crisis can force good appointments. The NPS survived a change of government because it was judged on its merits rather than its parentage.
stories.quote: This is the dream team of the people that had been leading the reforms all along.

stories.topic: A Half-Day Tutorial for Rahul Gandhi
stories.summary: Bibek Debroy organised a half-day at the Rajiv Gandhi Institute where Rahul Gandhi and a group of young Congress MPs went through pensions in detail with Ajay. They were engaged and asked detailed questions. Years later, Amit points out, the Congress campaigned state after state to bring back the OPS, even though its leadership had been walked through why it was disastrous.
stories.insight: Knowing the right answer doesn't stop politicians from pandering when incentives point the other way. Briefing leaders is not enough; there has to be pressure from public discourse.
stories.quote: they were interested and they asked all kinds of detailed questions and I explained the whole story to them to the best of my ability.

stories.topic: Fourteen Insurance CEOs vs Surendra Dave
stories.summary: The insurance industry pushed back against the NPS: pensions are insurance, so leave it to us, and we can do index funds and even guarantees. Chidambaram called a meeting with 14 insurance CEOs. Ajay was allowed to attend but told that 'measly junior people' were not there to debate. After each CEO made his pitch, Chidambaram turned to Surendra Dave, who gave what Ajay calls a masterly 15-minute rebuttal while Ajay's heart was in his mouth. Nobody replied. Chidambaram and Dave went off to confer, and later that day word came that the NPS was going ahead. Ajay's underlying point is that in an insurer's hands, pensions slide back into defined benefit.
stories.insight: Incumbents will try to absorb a new design into their old business model. One well-argued rebuttal at the right table can settle the matter.
stories.quote: Chidambaram and Dave left. They went and discussed a little more, and later in the day we were informed, boss has decided we're doing NPS.

stories.summary: Chidambaram wanted a law to make the NPS hard to reverse and to give the PFRDA regulatory teeth. But the CPI(M), essential to UPA-1, was doctrinaire about defined-benefit pensions. Negotiations dragged on from 2004 to 2009. Even after 2009, when the Congress could have carried the bill alone, it kept seeking consensus, and the law passed only in 2013. Meanwhile Chidambaram ran the NPS from 2004 through contracts with the fund managers and NSDL. Anyone who wanted the business had to agree to inspections and disclosure, so it was effectively regulation by private contract.
stories.insight: When legislation is blocked, clever legal engineering can still build state capacity. Even so, the NPS took 15 years to go from committee to law.
stories.quote: So what would be done in the bill as a regulatory arrangement was done through private contract

stories.topic: The Callow Youth Who Didn't Get Law
stories.summary: UK Sinha, who led the drafting of the PFRDA law, kept inviting young Ajay to every meeting and asking for his thoughts. Ajay admits he would just nod unintelligently. Only after the FSLRC did he understand law at a deeper level, and today he can see a hundred things the law could have done better.
stories.insight: Economics expertise isn't legal expertise. Generous seniors who keep juniors in the room build capability for the future.
stories.quote: I want to say I was a callow youth then and I did not understand laws.

stories.summary: When Ajay raised inflation targeting with Yashwant Sinha in 2002-03, Sinha said it was too far from conventional Indian intellectual discourse: 'Your baradari is not ready for this.' He said the economists of India had to come around first, and that he could only follow that consensus, not lead it. Inflation targeting finally arrived in 2015.
stories.insight: Even a finance minister can't get far ahead of the intellectual consensus. Real change comes from shifting what the community believes.
stories.quote: Then who am I? I'm a mere finance minister. I can only follow. I can't lead.

stories.topic: The Reform Community That Went Home
stories.summary: Around the 2002-04 decisions there was a lively pension reforms community, producing papers, seminars and op-eds. Once the NPS was in place, it disbanded. Pension work moved from KP Krishnan's DEA to the DFS, and institutional memory was lost; NIPFP had no working link with the DFS or PFRDA. Small problems festered: too little equity exposure, unresolved questions such as late joiners, and military pensions dropped, which later turned into OROP. Young civil servants in some states began demanding the OPS. Ajay once spent a day with Karnataka's trade unions at the state's informal request, walking through calculations. That kind of engagement then stopped happening.
stories.insight: Winning a reform is the start, not the end. Without a sustained community to fix flaws and keep persuading, even a sound reform decays.
stories.quote: Now, in hindsight, the biggest tragedy was that that community disbanded.

stories.summary: In the late 1990s Ajay pushed for the NPS to use cheap, competitively procured index funds instead of star fund managers. He lost many friends in the financial system, who had the machismo of 'I run money' and 'if you pay peanuts, you will get monkeys.' He argued that the expense ratio is the only thing to care about. He also argued that index funds suit government: there is no CBI investigation when a manager underperforms, and managers can be chosen transparently by tender.
stories.insight: The boring option can be the wise one, both financially and politically.
stories.quote: And the only test of an index fund is how little do you charge me.

recommendations.item: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
recommendations.context: Amit points viewers to it at the start as the earlier, detailed pensions episode, recorded while Congress was pushing to bring back the OPS in various states.
recommendations.reason: A longer audio deep-dive into the OPS-to-NPS story, with Renuka Sane, who spent recent years working on the NPS.

recommendations.item: Jayaprakash Narayan Wants to Mend Our Democracy (Episode 334, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
recommendations.context: Amit's third conversation with JP, where JP named pensions as the issue keeping him up at night.
recommendations.reason: The conversation that alerted Amit to the pensions crisis in the first place.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Recommended right after Ajay's behind-the-scenes stories of cabinet meetings and the politics of the NPS.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls this eight-hour episode an 'absolute masterpiece' on how the state works inside: what happens behind the scenes and what cabinet meetings are like.

recommendations.context: The expert committee led by Surendra Dave, which Ajay served on, that produced the NPS design.
recommendations.reason: The founding document of Indian pension reform: individual accounts, cheap index funds and a defined-contribution structure.

recommendations.item: Towards Estimating India's Implicit Pension Debt (2005)
recommendations.creator: Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave
recommendations.context: The calculation behind the 68%-of-GDP figure for promises made to civil servants.
recommendations.reason: It reframed pensions from a growing yearly bill into a giant stock of debt and woke up the political leadership. Ajay laments that it was never repeated.

recommendations.item: Investment Risk in Indian Pension Sector and Role for Pension Guarantees (2003)
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions his paper on pension guarantees while analysing the UPS's 50% guarantee.
recommendations.reason: It frames pension guarantees as put options on the portfolio, which can be very expensive. That is the lens for asking whether the UPS is affordable.

recommendations.creator: Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited while criticising the UPS for coming without published calculations.
recommendations.reason: A model of transparent policy analysis: all source code and assumptions are published, so readers can change the inputs and rerun the numbers themselves.

recommendations.item: A sustainable and scalable approach in Indian pension reform (2005)
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Writing from the period when the pension reforms community was active, which is the kind of research flow the episode argues reforms need.

recommendations.creator: Renuka Sane and Susan Thomas

recommendations.creator: Renuka Sane and William Price
recommendations.reason: An example of the ongoing pension simulation work Ajay says India needed far more of.

recommendations.item: There be dragons: Off-balance-sheet liabilities of the Indian State (2018)
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Companion reading on hidden liabilities like the possible UPS guarantee, which Ajay describes as a contingent liability dangling over the Indian state.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Pointed to after Ajay ties falling fertility to pensions.
recommendations.reason: It argues that India's problem is too few children, not too many. That directly undermines pension promises that assume lots of young workers and short-lived retirees.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay links pensions to state capability and military reform.
recommendations.reason: It shows why fixing military pensions is the first item on any agenda for building a capable modern military.

recommendations.reason: It sets out the view that reform comes slowly, through shifting the intellectual consensus rather than whispering in officials' ears.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit applies structural vs parametric reform to personal life.
recommendations.reason: His example of a structural reform in one's own life: changing what you eat and how you eat, rather than tweaking at the margins.

recommendations.creator: James Clear
recommendations.context: Amit's end-of-episode recommendation, following the 'reform thyself' discussion.
recommendations.reason: It teaches you to turn away from goals and towards habits and processes, which is a structural reform for your own life.

core_ideas.explanation: Life expectancy at birth (around 74 in India) misleads pension thinking. Once you survive to 60 or 70, every way you could have died earlier is behind you, so your expected remaining life is longer than the headline number suggests. Pensions must be valued over roughly a 100-year horizon: a 20-year-old today has a reasonable chance of reaching 120. That means using forward-looking longevity projections, not backward-looking LIC death data.
core_ideas.quote: Once you've made it to 60, you actually have more years to go. Once you've made it to 70, you have more years to go because it's a conditional expectation.

core_ideas.concept: Three Forces That Wreck Defined-Benefit Pensions
core_ideas.explanation: Bismarck-style promises were cheap because people died soon and young workers were plentiful. Three forces broke them. Longevity rose, so payments run for more years. Fertility fell, so the population pyramid turned into a barrel, with fewer young people paying for more old people. And democratic politics kept loosening the terms: lower ages, higher percentages, more indexation.
core_ideas.quote: The fudge factors, like should it be a fifty percent pension, should it be age seventy, these numbers kept getting modified year after year in a more reckless way under the pressure of democratic politics.

core_ideas.explanation: A defined-benefit (DB) pension guarantees a fixed payment for life. Ajay speaks as a 'one-handed economist' here, with no 'on the other hand'. There is no healthy DB programme anywhere in the world, and governments, including rich-country governments, have repeatedly broken these promises. So the young civil servants demanding the OPS are chasing a promise that is likely to fail them too.
core_ideas.quote: Every single defined benefit program in the world has got into trouble. There is not one defined benefit program that has stayed out of trouble.

core_ideas.concept: Nominal vs Inflation-Indexed vs Wage-Indexed: Chalk and Cheese
core_ideas.explanation: These sound like jargon variants but cost wildly different amounts. A nominal pension (a fixed 50 rupees) is roughly achievable with sound financial planning. An inflation-indexed pension is roughly a doubling of the present value and only partly achievable. A wage-indexed pension (50% of what someone in your old job earns today) is astronomically expensive and impossible to fund prudently. Intuitions of fair play, as in OROP's 'a general should get the same pension whenever he retired', blur these differences and blow up the cost.
core_ideas.quote: There does not exist a wise management strategy through which wage indexation can be obtained.

core_ideas.concept: Defined Contribution: Coerce Saving, Not Transfers
core_ideas.explanation: In a defined-contribution (DC) pension, the state's coercion only forces you to put your own money into your own account. Nobody pays for anybody else, and each person plans for the old age they want. Ajay calls socialisation the root of all evil here. DB pensions, by contrast, are payments from the young to the old. They set generations against each other in organised class warfare.
core_ideas.quote: State coercion is used to put money into a pension account. Beyond that, each person is free and each person is on her own.

core_ideas.concept: Implicit Pension Debt: Stock vs Flow
core_ideas.explanation: Watching this year's pension payouts (the flow) hides the danger. Take the present value of every promise already made and you get a stock of debt. That is how much the state would need to borrow to buy annuities for all current workers and pensioners. For India's civil servants alone this came to 68% of GDP; Ajay puts the US figure at 200% of GDP. Ajay calls it a tragedy that India never repeated the calculation after Bhardwaj and Dave.
core_ideas.quote: When you NPV the promises to civil servants, that gives you a number which is like a stock of debt.

core_ideas.concept: Pensions as a Test of State Capability
core_ideas.explanation: Like winning a war, getting pensions right is a raw test of whether a state can think. It has to make 100-year calculations and stay responsible under political pressure. Military pensions in particular are make-or-break: without fixing them and moving soldiers into the NPS, there is no money for a modern, skilled military.
core_ideas.quote: Ponder this sentence that a mighty military is made out of economics, and the first problem on the agenda of Indian military reform is solve this damn pensions mess.

core_ideas.explanation: Here is how the NPS works. 20% of salary is compulsorily deducted into a personal account that is the individual's private property, and on death it passes to the next of kin. A small pool of fund managers (six were intended) is picked by public tender and runs dumb, cheap index funds across equities, corporate bonds and government bonds. An expert committee sets the default allocation, and the default money goes to the lowest-cost manager. Individuals can override the allocation and switch managers frictionlessly online. A central record-keeping utility (NSDL) and the NPS Trust hold everything together.
core_ideas.quote: it's my money being kept in an account. For me. Okay, like nobody else gets their claws on that money.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian finance runs on the toxic maxim 'fund management is sold, not bought'. That means celebrity ads with Shah Rukh Khan, crazy commissions, and armies of LIC-style agents herding people like lemmings into tax-saving products. The NPS inverts this. There are no sales campaigns, and fund managers get wholesale pools of money without even knowing who their customers are. Their only job is to run an index fund at the lowest price.
core_ideas.quote: There's a phrase in finance which is a deeply toxic one which says that fund management is sold, not bought.

core_ideas.explanation: From age 20 to retirement, pension saving is just fund management: your money, no pooling, no actuarial calculations. Insurance enters only at the end, if you choose to convert your lump sum into a monthly annuity. Handing the whole system to insurance companies would let it slide back into defined benefit, which is why their lobby had to be resisted.
core_ideas.quote: It is only at the end that people choose that do you want to take a stock of money and turn it into a predictable monthly payment? That is an insurance step, and only that should be with insurance companies.

core_ideas.concept: Pension Money Serves Only the Pensioner
core_ideas.explanation: Pension policy should have one objective: the welfare of the people whose money it is. It should not prop up the stock market or fund infrastructure. By that test, Ajay's one regret about the NPS design is that it should have been globally diversified from day one. Global diversification roughly halves risk, so perhaps 60-80% should be invested abroad. Separately, civil servants' failure of nerve kept equity exposure too low, even though equities delivered astounding returns over the last two decades.
core_ideas.quote: No other objective should be brought into the picture. We should be good to the individuals who are participating in the NPS. That's our only objective.

core_ideas.concept: Fair Transitions: Grandfather, Then Pay Double for a Generation
core_ideas.explanation: The NPS did not touch promises already made: anyone hired even a month earlier kept the OPS, and only new recruits joined the NPS, with the terms clear from the job advertisement. The cost of fairness is that for about a generation the state pays twice. It pays old-scheme pensions and also the higher wages of new joiners. The fiscal payoff only arrives around 2029. Without anyone keeping that long view alive, impatient governments gave up just before the gains arrived.
core_ideas.quote: by its very design, the NPS reform involved a one generation problem that for one generation governments are paying double.

core_ideas.concept: Reforms Need a Standing Intellectual Ecosystem
core_ideas.explanation: Policymakers respond to incentives. On one side stand a few lakh organised civil servants. If no researchers, papers, calculations or op-eds stand on the other side, politicians will pander, even when, as Amit notes, they know it hurts the country. A pension reform community made the NPS possible, and its disbanding is why the NPS is being undone. Ajay argues that governments and philanthropists should fund such communities and require data to be released to them.
core_ideas.quote: A country can only be as good as its intellectuals.

core_ideas.concept: Theory of Change: Move the Overton Window, Don't Whisper in Ears
core_ideas.explanation: A popular theory of change in India is to sidle up to a joint secretary, or fund young English-speaking staff and consultants for them. That only achieves small things inside the existing consensus. Real reform comes from legitimising complex ideas across the wider intellectual community until policymakers can act on them.
core_ideas.quote: The point, however, is to change the Overton window, is to legitimize the complex reforms that are needed in the country that are beyond the horizon of an average policymaker.

core_ideas.concept: The UPS Guarantee Is a Put Option
core_ideas.explanation: The UPS fixes some genuine NPS problems. But its 50% guarantee works like a put option on each worker's portfolio: a minimum payout regardless of market conditions, which can be very expensive to provide. Its partial inflation indexation also assumes inflation-indexed annuities that India's market doesn't offer. No calculations have been published, so it may be a large contingent liability on the state, and at present nobody can tell.
core_ideas.quote: So it could be a contingent liability that is dangling upon the Indian State. And at present we don't know.

core_ideas.explanation: Decisions involving liabilities worth tens of percent of GDP should come with published numbers. Ajay and Renuka Sane's OROP analysis released all its code and assumptions, so anyone could rerun it with different inputs. Ajay sees that as the only path to real democratic deliberation, and the UPS falls short of it.
core_ideas.quote: So you're welcome to download the code, change the assumptions, run it yourself. You know, that's the pathway to a meaningful deliberative democratic discourse

core_ideas.explanation: A parametric reform keeps the old machine and twiddles its dials. Over time politics will twiddle them the wrong way. A structural reform builds a clean engine with no dials to fiddle. The NPS was structural: it is just your money in your account. The warnings are NREGS, promised as self-liquidating, whose wage kept rising and which now permanently distorts the labour market, and government healthcare, where package promises would keep ratcheting up. Whoever turns the knobs well today will be gone in a few years.
core_ideas.quote: In parametric reforms, we hold a basic edifice intact and twiddle with some dials. In structural reform, we create a clean engine and that engine suffers from a lack of those kinds of dials, so it is likely to work better.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit turns the structural-vs-parametric frame onto personal life. Locking yourself away for a weekend to write, or sprinting occasionally while unfit, is a parametric tweak. Building daily habits, so that a marathon becomes easy, is structural. His challenge to listeners is to ask what is wrong with their own life and which kind of reform it needs.
core_ideas.quote: We talk here about reforming the state. I tell the reader, reform thyself.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on why he started out in audio: 'I have always thought I have a face for audio, which is why the Seen and the Unseen Audio Podcast.' Doing video with the 'good looking and dashing' Ajay forced him to shave, which started the whole bloody affair.

Amit, bleeding from a shaving cut: 'Just as this nation is regrettably too full of bleeding heart liberals, here you had a bleeding lip libertarian. Though I do not like labels, Pushpa, so we shall not go there.'

Amit on the blood trailing down his chest: 'Had my torso been a little more better developed, it would have been an exceptionally enticing scene, but it wasn't. It was just bloody.' Following Ajay's advice to stand in front of a fan, he became 'perhaps the first person in history to aim a hairdryer at his lips.'

Harry Truman's plea, 'Give me a one-handed economist': he was tired of advisers saying 'on one hand this, on the other hand that.' Ajay declares himself one-handed on defined-benefit pensions, and Amit explains the line.

Amit's version of wage indexation: 'After I retire, I want the state to give me every month half of BeerBiceps' income... That's where I want it indexed.' Then, to be clear: 'As far as money is concerned, I'm not doing his content.'
Ajay on the tabloid nightmare policymakers sandbag against: 'Oh, this person was a secretary to government and now she's sitting by the gates of the Bangalore Metro begging for a free idli sambar.'

Ajay on why index funds suit government: if a discretionary fund manager does badly, 'they will want a CBI investigation.' His fund-manager friends' machismo, 'If you pay peanuts, you will get monkeys', cost him many of those friendships.
Ajay voicing the insurance lobby: 'We don't want no stinking pension fund managers, we don't want no stinking index funds... we, the insurance industry, will do it.'
Ajay on Vajpayee in meetings: he had a way of either appearing to be asleep or actually being asleep, 'and you could never tell, but he was a wise man.'

After Ajay recounts being told 'measly junior people like you are not here to debate', Amit to the audience: 'Gentle reader, this person here who looks like an elder statesman was once a firebrand revolutionary, right? You haven't seen that side of him.'
Amit pitching a web series on pensions, with a critical scene of Ajay in the PMO and Vajpayee 'looking at you slowly in his languorous, leisurely way' as Ajay does his projections.
Ajay on states trying to grab NPS money: 'last I heard it was not yet easy for governments in India to expropriate our private property. I mean I know they can do it, but it is still hard.'
'Yeh to karna hi hai' ('This simply has to be done'), Vajpayee's ruling that settled the NPS debate in cabinet. Ajay proposes it as the slogan for every reformer in India.
Milton Friedman's matrix of spending, recalled from the EIE public choice episode: the state is 'spending other people's money on other people', so nothing forces it to be responsible.
Amit on the reform community's complacency: 'to use Jefferson's alleged phrase, eternal vigilance is still required.'
Ajay, 26 years after Project Oasis, twisting Mark Antony's line: 'I come to praise the NPS, not bury it.'
